1.note: Every hydrogen atom in your body is about 13.8 billion years old.

2.note: Most helium in the universe is from the Big Bang, but the helium in party balloons comes from rocks: alpha particles from decaying uranium and thorium, trapped underground with natural gas.
2.earth: On Earth, the helium people extract is mostly from radioactive decay in rocks.

3.note: Lithium is the odd one out: the Big Bang made some, cosmic rays a little, and dying stars most of the rest, yet stars also destroy it, so there is far less than models first predicted.

4.note: Stars destroy beryllium rather than make it. Nearly all of it comes from cosmic rays smashing carbon, nitrogen and oxygen nuclei in space.

5.note: Most boron is chipped off heavier nuclei by cosmic rays; some boron-11 is made by the neutrino blast of exploding stars.

6.note: About half of your carbon was puffed out by dying Sun-like stars, half by massive stars.

8.note: The oxygen you breathe was forged inside massive stars and blasted out when they exploded.

18.note: On Earth, 99.6% of argon is argon-40, made in rocks by the radioactive decay of potassium-40. That is why our air holds so much of it.
18.earth: On Earth, argon is almost all from the radioactive decay of potassium-40.

26.note: Iron comes from two kinds of supernova: exploding white dwarfs make a little more than half, collapsing massive stars the rest.

43.note: Technetium has no stable isotope. Any it was born with decayed long ago; tiny traces form in uranium ores, but almost all of it on Earth is made in nuclear reactors.
43.earth: On Earth: human-made in reactors; natural traces form from uranium fission.

47.note: Silver is mostly from the rapid neutron capture of merging neutron stars, the same violent process that made gold.

56.note: Barium is a classic slow neutron-capture element, built a neutron at a time inside dying red giant stars over thousands of years.

61.note: Promethium has no stable isotope. A few hundred grams exist in Earth’s crust at any moment, from uranium fission; what people use is made in reactors.
61.earth: On Earth: human-made in reactors; natural traces form from uranium fission.

63.note: Europium is the textbook tracer of the rapid neutron-capture process, so astronomers use it to track neutron-star mergers through cosmic history.

79.note: Most of the gold in your jewellery was made when two neutron stars collided, before the Sun was born.

82.note: Most lead was built slowly in dying red giants, and some on Earth is the end point of uranium and thorium decay.

84.note: On Earth, polonium only exists because uranium keeps decaying in rocks. Marie Curie found it in that decay chain.
84.earth: On Earth: produced continuously by the decay of uranium and thorium, which came from merging neutron stars.

85.earth: On Earth: produced continuously by the decay of uranium and thorium.

86.note: Radon seeps out of the ground because uranium in rocks is always decaying into it.
86.earth: On Earth: produced continuously by the decay of uranium and thorium.

87.earth: On Earth: produced continuously by the decay of uranium (about 30 g exists in the crust at any moment).

88.earth: On Earth: produced continuously by the decay of uranium and thorium.

89.earth: On Earth: produced continuously by the decay of uranium and thorium.

90.note: Thorium and uranium were made by merging neutron stars before the Solar System formed. Their slow decay still heats Earth’s interior today.

91.earth: On Earth: produced continuously by the decay of uranium.

92.note: Uranium was made by merging neutron stars billions of years ago, and it is still decaying. Earth’s uranium is a cosmic clock.

93.earth: Traces form naturally in uranium ores, but almost all neptunium is made in reactors.

94.earth: Traces form naturally in uranium ores, but almost all plutonium is made in reactors.
